item.title: Under Secretary Helberg’s Travel to Singapore, Indonesia, and Japan
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Under Secretary Helberg’s Travel to Singapore, Indonesia, and Japan

Media Note

November 9, 2026

Under Secretary of State for Economic Affairs Jacob S. Helberg traveled to Singapore, Indonesia, and Japan October 28 to November 7 to connect American technological leadership with the capital, industrial capabilities, and ambitions of U.S. partners in the Indo-Pacific.

In Singapore, Under Secretary Helberg met with government and industry leaders to expand the use of American Super Intelligence (SI) technologies while keeping advanced capabilities secure.  Singapore’s new agreements with American companies will help bring U.S. frontier models into public services and business applications across Southeast Asia.

In Indonesia, Under Secretary Helberg met with government and industry leaders to advance discussions on more than $2 billion in prospective U.S. commercial deals in energy and information and communications technology.  They also discussed further cooperation on secure supply chains and industrial development that would create opportunities for American companies to contribute to Indonesia’s growth.

In Japan, Under Secretary Helberg deepened dialogue with government and industry leaders on critical minerals, semiconductors, energy, and compute.  The Under Secretary met with robotics, undersea cable, and semiconductor equipment manufacturers.  The meetings focused on industrial productivity, next-generation communications, protection of advanced technology, and promoting further investment in the United States.

item.title: Secretary Rubio’s Meeting with French Foreign Minister Barrot
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Secretary Rubio’s Meeting with French Foreign Minister Barrot

Readout

November 9, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met today with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot.  The Secretary and Foreign Minister discussed U.S. fundamental concerns about the International Criminal Court.

The Secretary and Foreign Minister also addressed the situation in the Middle East, reaffirming the importance of freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.  The Secretary also called for the cessation of EU preference measures and overregulation targeting U.S. companies.

Lastly, they discussed efforts to secure a durable, long-term peace settlement to the Russia-Ukraine war.

Secretary Rubio’s Meeting with German Foreign Minister Wadephul

Readout

November 9, 2026

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul during the G7 Foreign Ministers Meeting in Paris, France.  The two leaders discussed bilateral efforts to secure freedom of navigation, strengthen defense industrial cooperation, and deepen our trade relationship.  Secretary Rubio also commended recent contributions from the German government to the Gang Suppression Force in Haiti.

item.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Homestead, Florida

Homestead Air Reserve Base

Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press

Remarks

November 8, 2026

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah. 

QUESTION:  There’s this report out just now that India is going to be investigating CEO Jensen Huang.  New York Times reported that you had concerns about his relationship with the Chinese spy.  Can you bring us up to date as to if Jensen Huang was cut out of any U.S. Government meetings or any briefings as a result —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I can’t comment on any of that.  I just can’t comment because of the nature of it.  And I also can’t comment on an internal corporate matter that’s going on with Nvidia (inaudible) I don’t know anything about that part of it so —

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, what lesson can you take from the midterm elections (inaudible) when it comes to your foreign policy —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’m not in a political office.  As you know, I just don’t comment on domestic politics. 

QUESTION:  Can you say —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Sorry to be less than exciting with regard to that; it’s a new thing for me after having spent 14 years doing it.  But I think this role is best done for the most part when you don’t engage yourself in domestic politics.  I think it’s been a longstanding tradition.  So —

QUESTION:  Do you agree with the Vice President when he says (inaudible) war should end?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, I’m not going to comment on the war – or, I’m sorry, on the elections, which is what you’re asking me about.  All I can tell you is that the President of the United States identified a very real threat to this country that’s existed for a very long period of time, and he addressed it.  And he addressed it even though, oftentimes, the right thing to do for the country – confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country – doing it isn’t necessarily popular but necessary.  At the end of the day I think we all can all agree, I think there’s bipartisan – I would hope there’s bipartisan – maybe not anymore – but there used to be bipartisan acknowledgment that a nuclear Iran would be completely unacceptable and dangerous for the United States – not just Israel, not just the Middle East – the whole world and the United States. 

So I think the President took on something that other presidents have failed to do.  And sometimes when you do the right thing – I don’t know if it’s popular or not, but it’s the right thing to do.  And presidents are elected to do the hard things – sometimes difficult things, but necessary things.

QUESTION:  Do you believe the cost of the war was worth the electoral blowout?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I told you I’m not going to comment on electoral – I just don’t have any opinion on what happened in the election. 

QUESTION:  On the two kind of active conflicts you have now, there’s been more sort of – more strikes on Qeshm Island, the —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, the U.S. acts defensively.  If there’s a threat to our forces in the region, we will act against those.  If there’s a threat to shipping, we’ve been defending shipping for a while.  So if there’s a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves.  So all of that is determined by the threat level and whether they’re coming after us or potentially coming after us.  But I mean, that’s just normal —

QUESTION:  And then on Ukraine, Russia-Ukraine, the President floated this idea of some kind of European-wide security pact.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, if you remember —

QUESTION:  I was just wondering if this is going to be —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Well, there’ll be talks tomorrow, starting tomorrow, in Abu Dhabi.

QUESTION:  No, I mean at the G7.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Oh, I’m sure.  What – because here’s why.  The entirety of the time we’ve been talking about Russia-Ukraine, the one thing that’s repeatedly come up is the need for security guarantees – what is the post-war security infrastructure of Ukraine and, more broadly, of the European continent going to look like?  And it’s one of the key topics that’s been raised repeatedly in every conversation any time negotiations have been discussed.  So I think that’s what the President is alluding to, that there’s been some advances made in what that architecture should look like post-conflict.  We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point.

So look, there’s been talks about that.  I think the President was briefed on that on Thursday or Friday of last week, some of the initial thoughts that are out there.  Nothing’s been finalized yet.  And maybe some progress can be made in Abu Dhabi tomorrow when Jared and Steve will be there.  I think they’re on the way there right now.

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary, I know you don’t want to comment on the elections but —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  But you’re going to ask me anyway.

QUESTION:  — but your allies are going to ask you about it tomorrow, because it’s your first opportunity that you all meet inside the G7 after the election.

SECRETARY RUBIO:  We have – we have national elections in our country every two years.  I have been now involved, I guess going since 2011 when I was sworn in as a senator, so I’ve watched these things – and even my time in the legislature.  It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country.  We’ve seen it before.  We’ve seen elections going one direction and, a couple years later, go another.  It’s just a feature of our system.  So I’ve been in the minority, I’ve been in the majority, with regards to being in the Senate.  I’ve been in the majority with a Republican president.  I’ve been in the minority with a Democrat president.  I think I’ve had every iteration of it.  And the Republican (inaudible) continues. 

So we’ll do our work; we’ll continue to do our work.  Congress will do theirs.  I hope they do it in a way that’s responsible and focused on the issues that are important to our country and our people.  But that’s our system of government.  Many of our allies will be aware but they too have experienced divisions in government and divisions in their own system.  So we’ll have elections again in two more years.  And they could look very different; they could look the same.  I don’t know.  But this is the way our system works.

QUESTION:  Is there a particular message you’re looking to bring to allies on this trip? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  On – with regards to this trip?  Well, they have an agenda the French have set.  Obviously, we’ll be talking about super intelligence.  We’ll be talking about some of the global conflicts.  I’m sure they’ll have a lot of questions about the status of affairs in the Middle East with regards to Iran.  I think there’ll be, obviously, a conversation.  The Ukrainians are joining us; Sybiha will be there.  So I’m sure that topic will come up.  I know – I think they’ll be curious to know of any progress that’s being made in the technical talks that are ongoing in Abu Dhabi. 

And then I imagine there’s a host of other issues they’ll want to discuss.  But the agenda, you’ll see it.  I mean, it’s been pretty – it’s been laid out, some of the topics they want to raise and talk about.  So —

QUESTION:  Mr. Secretary —

QUESTION:  You’re going to France.  Is there any worry about the protests that’s been happening there?

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No.  I mean, I trust our people.  I mean, we asked our people, obviously.  If there was a problem, I think they would tell us.  So we got to – the work must continue, right.  I mean, France has the presidency.  I think this is probably the last meeting in the G7 under their presidency in terms of foreign ministers.  And I think we’ll host it next year.  So yeah, I – if  our people say it’s fine, I believe them.  So —

QUESTION:  Any diplomatic progress with Iran for drawing a diplomatic end to the war? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I don’t have any progress to report to you.  I think you see some of these things that are out there; you have a number of countries that continue to engage them with different ideas.  But I wouldn’t say we’re in – on the verge of a breakthrough.  The President would always prefer to solve this and every problem diplomatically.  Sometimes that’s not possible, unfortunately.  But if there’s a chance to do it, we’ll explore it.  Right now it hasn’t been very productive, because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable but, in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.

All right? Let me go do my call —

QUESTION:  Just on Haiti quickly, sir —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Haiti?

QUESTION:  Yeah, the Salvadorian deployments that have gone in there.  The President said – he kind of green-lit that, but is the U.S. providing any support?  And are you concerned that —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, I mean, the – I think – no, I mean, the Salvadorians are providing their own airlift.  So there’s two things going on in Haiti.  We have the gang suppression force, which is the UN mission, and they have forces – I think about a hundred soldiers that are a part of that.  And that’s what we’ve been engaged in and supporting.  We don’t have troops there, but we’ve been engaged.

And then there’s a separate mission, which they’ve taken on bilaterally in agreement with the Haitian officials, to go after the gangs that kidnapped their forces that were there, their soldiers that were there.  So that’s a separate mission.  He called the President and made them aware of what he was doing, and the President understood why he was doing it.  But we’re not necessarily – we’re not actively involved in that effort. 

QUESTION:  Does it potentially undermine the gang suppression force that you have? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  No, as long —

QUESTION:  The Salvadoreans that you have there —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah. 

QUESTION:  — are private security contractors.  There’s a lot of people in the ground working. 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah.  No, as long as the chain of command is well established, who’s working for who.  And I think they’ll have to – and we’ve raised this point, not because it’s a criticism, just as an observation.  We have to make – we have to make sure that there’s de-confliction going on.  What you can’t have is gang suppression force running into Salvadorian soldiers and shooting at each other because they think the other side are gang members.  So that’s why you’ll need a de-confliction mechanism.  You’ll need a lot of strong coordination because they’re operating alongside one another.  So we pointed that out, and – but I don’t think it necessarily has to be a conflict.  Okay?

QUESTION:  (Inaudible) —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah. 

QUESTION:  We’re now into the fifth-month —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Period – right. 

QUESTION:  — period before the sanctions begin against (inaudible).  And what is your – is your demand of your allies to be able to make this (inaudible) —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Or – unless they can get them to change their mind and agree to reform, as they should. 

QUESTION:  But what —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  They should make very clear that they do not – you still have elements of the ICC who claim that they have jurisdiction over citizens that are not – of non-member-states.  And we’re never going to accept that when it comes to Americans.  It’s as simple as that.  We’ve been clear on that.  For a year and a half, we’ve made no progress trying to get them to make that clear in their reforms.  They refuse to do so, so we’re taking action.  And that’s it.

QUESTION:  Is that what you want to see in writing from the (inaudible) by your allies, some sort of change (inaudible) —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I mean, at this point, we’ve made clear to them where we stand on it and how we feel about it.  And we’ve asked them, if they don’t want us to take these actions against the ICC, then they should convince the ICC to wake up and realize that they do not have jurisdiction over citizens of countries that are not members, especially leaders or a servicemember of countries that are not members of the treaty.  What’s the point of the treaty?  If they claim universal jurisdiction without limitation and outside the treaty, then they’re way outside the bounds of their – of the mandate that they may have from these other countries that are members of it. 

So it’s very simple.  If they want to avoid the actions we are going to take against the ICC, they should convince the ICC once and for all to do the things that are necessary to ensure that no American servicemember or leader ever has jurisdiction from the ICC placed on them because that’s illegitimate.  It’s an illegitimate action.  And they refuse to acknowledge that.  So we’ll do what we need to do if they don’t do it.

All right. 

QUESTION:  So how big a problem would it be if they invoked the (inaudible) of the EU, (inaudible) secondary sanctions? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’m not concerned.  We won’t have – we have our ways; we’ll get to it.  The ICC will not be in good shape if we have to get there.  And we will if we have to.  But look, they still have a chance.  Maybe they’ll wake up and realize that their dreams of being some universal court of jurisdiction over everyone, including countries that didn’t sign up, maybe they’ll abandon those ridiculous dreams.  We’ll see.  We’re on it. 

Okay, thanks, guys. 

QUESTION:  Thank you.

QUESTION:  But what —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  They should make very clear that they do not – you still have elements of the ICC who claim that they have jurisdiction over citizens that are not – of non-member-states.  And we’re never going to accept that when it comes to Americans.  It’s as simple as that.  We’ve been clear on that.  For a year and a half, we’ve made no progress trying to get them to make that clear in their reforms.  They refuse to do so, so we’re taking action.  And that’s it.

QUESTION:  Is that what you want to see in writing from the (inaudible) by your allies, some sort of change (inaudible) —

SECRETARY RUBIO:  Yeah, I mean, at this point, we’ve made clear to them where we stand on it and how we feel about it.  And we’ve asked them, if they don’t want us to take these actions against the ICC, then they should convince the ICC to wake up and realize that they do not have jurisdiction over citizens of countries that are not members, especially leaders or a servicemember of countries that are not members of the treaty.  What’s the point of the treaty?  If they claim universal jurisdiction without limitation and outside the treaty, then they’re way outside the bounds of their – of the mandate that they may have from these other countries that are members of it. 

So it’s very simple.  If they want to avoid the actions we are going to take against the ICC, they should convince the ICC once and for all to do the things that are necessary to ensure that no American servicemember or leader ever has jurisdiction from the ICC placed on them because that’s illegitimate.  It’s an illegitimate action.  And they refuse to acknowledge that.  So we’ll do what we need to do if they don’t do it.

All right. 

QUESTION:  So how big a problem would it be if they invoked the (inaudible) of the EU, (inaudible) secondary sanctions? 

SECRETARY RUBIO:  I’m not concerned.  We won’t have – we have our ways; we’ll get to it.  The ICC will not be in good shape if we have to get there.  And we will if we have to.  But look, they still have a chance.  Maybe they’ll wake up and realize that their dreams of being some universal court of jurisdiction over everyone, including countries that didn’t sign up, maybe they’ll abandon those ridiculous dreams.  We’ll see.  We’re on it. 

Okay, thanks, guys. 

QUESTION:  Thank you.

item.title: Cambodia National Day
item.dc:creator: Marco Rubio, Secretary of State
item.description:
Marco Rubio, Secretary of State

Cambodia National Day

Press Statement

November 8, 2026

On behalf of the United States of America, I congratulate the Kingdom of Cambodia as it celebrates its 73rd Independence Day.

The United States and Cambodia have built a close relationship based on trust, mutual respect, and shared interest for more than 75 years. President Trump’s leadership in helping broker the historic Kuala Lumpur Peace Accords has opened a new chapter in our relationship, creating opportunities to advance lasting peace and expand economic prosperity for Americans and the Cambodian people alike. We look forward to working together to support a strong and independent Cambodia.

I extend my warmest wishes to the people of Cambodia as you celebrate this important milestone in your nation’s history.

item.title: Joint Statement on the Launch of Trilateral Technical Planning Groups to Advance the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP)
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

Joint Statement on the Launch of Trilateral Technical Planning Groups to Advance the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP)

Media Note

November 6, 2026

The following text was released by the Governments of the United States of America, Armenia, and Azerbaijan.

Begin Text.

Today, U.S. Assistant Secretary of State for European and Eurasian Affairs Brendan Hanrahan, Armenian Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Trade Vahan Kostanyan, and Azerbaijani Deputy Foreign Minister Elnur Mammadov launched Trilateral Technical Planning Groups to advance the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a multimodal transit route. This forum brings together policymakers and technical experts from our three countries to work collaboratively and contribute to long-term stability, economic vitality, regional connectivity, and commercial prosperity across the region, underscoring the landmark August 8, 2025, Peace Summit Declaration brokered by President Trump.

Demonstrating a shared commitment to turn vision into tangible progress, the parties agreed to inaugurate the first two Trilateral Planning Groups focused on transportation and electricity transmission. These technical planning groups represent a crucial step toward resolving complex technical issues and moving to the next phases of implementation, including connection with other regional infrastructures.

The sides reaffirmed their respective commitments to expeditious operationalization of all modalities of TRIPP.

End Text.

item.title: U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime
item.dc:creator: Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman
item.description:
Thomas "Tommy" Pigott, SpokesmanOffice of the Spokesman

U.S. Sanctions Cripple Financial Networks Sustaining the Iranian Regime

Press Statement

November 6, 2026

The United States is taking action today against eight digital asset service providers that help the Iranian regime evade sanctions and fund terrorism. The Department of the Treasury is designating these firms, which exchange Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets so that the regime, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and other sanctioned actors can move money into and out of Iran.

Several of these businesses sent funds to digital asset accounts linked to the IRGC and other terrorist activity. Many also dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges that the United States has already sanctioned. Some changed their names and addresses to avoid detection, and all of them kept operating despite public reporting on the risks they posed.

As part of Operation Economic Outcast, the United States will continue to cut off revenue the Iranian regime uses to fund terrorism, weapons proliferation, and its proxies across the Middle East. Today’s action deepens Iran’s economic isolation and targets its growing use of digital assets to get around sanctions. It follows U.S. sanctions earlier this year on Iranian digital asset exchanges that moved money for the regime and the IRGC. Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable.

The United States coordinated this action closely with Canada, including Canada’s financial intelligence unit, FINTRAC. It reflects our shared commitment to protecting the North American financial system from abuse. Several of the designated businesses also laundered proceeds from drug trafficking, which shows how the same illicit networks serve both Iran and criminal organizations that threaten the safety of our communities. We will keep working with Canada and other international partners to expose these networks, shut them down, and make sure no country becomes a refuge for people who finance terrorism and evade sanctions.

Today’s designations are imposed pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13902, which targets the Iranian digital asset sector, among other key sectors of the Iranian economy. For more information, please see Treasury’s press release.

item.title: U.S. Department of State Announces Selection for the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale
item.dc:creator: Office of the Spokesman
item.description:
Office of the Spokesman

U.S. Department of State Announces Selection for the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

Media Note

November 6, 2026

Today, the Department of State announced the selection of The University of Miami School of Architecture to represent the United States at the 20th Venice Architecture Biennale.  The 2027 U.S. Pavilion exhibition, Earth Craft, is organized by Lead Curator Germane Barnes, Associate Professor and Director of the Master of Architecture Graduate Program at the University of Miami School of Architecture and Principal of Studio Barnes.  The exhibition will look at how American architecture is shaped by the land and the people who build on it.  It will follow earthen materials, including brick, rammed earth, adobe, and concrete masonry, from the ground to the finished building.  It will also recognize the brickmakers, masons, and builders who used American soil to build the homes, schools, and public buildings found across the United States.  The Bureau of Educational and Cultural Affairs supports and manages the official U.S. participation at Venice Arts and Architecture Biennales to showcase the excellence of American art and culture on the world stage.

For additional information, please contact eca-press@state.gov.

Secretary Rubio’s Travel to France

Media Note

Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to Paris, France November 8-10. The Secretary will attend the G7 Foreign Ministers Meeting, where he will advance American interests in engagements with his G7 counterparts.
